paragraphs.source_en: The master's wife poured fresh tea, set it before Meitei, and said, “I am sorry to have kept you waiting. He will probably be back soon.” “Where has he gone?” “I do not know. He never says where he is going when he goes out. I suppose he has gone to the doctor.” “Dr. Amaki, is it? Dr. Amaki is unlucky to have got hold of a patient like him.” The master's wife seemed at a loss for an answer, and only gave a brief “Yes.” Meitei paid no attention to that and asked again, “How has he been lately? Is his stomach trouble a little better?” “Whether it is better or worse, I cannot make it out at all. No matter how often Dr. Amaki sees him, if he keeps licking jam the way he does, I do not think his stomach illness will ever get better.” The master's wife was privately pouring out to Meitei the resentment she had just felt toward her husband. “He is so fond of jam, he is just like a child.” “It is not only jam. Lately he has been eating grated radish like mad, saying it is medicine for his stomach trouble.” “Well, well!” Meitei exclaimed. The master's wife said, “He read in the newspaper, apparently, that there is diastase in radishes.” “I see! So that is his device for offsetting the jam. He really is ingenious. Ha, ha...” Hearing the master's wife's complaints, Meitei actually looked thoroughly delighted. “Why, the other day he even fed it to the baby.” The master's wife said. “Jam?” Meitei asked. “No, grated radish. Can you imagine it? He said, ‘Come here, little one, Father will give you something tasty.’ On the rare occasion that he shows affection for the children, he does nothing but such foolish things. Two or three days ago, he picked up our second daughter and put her on top of the chest of drawers...” “What sort of scheme had he thought up this time?” Whatever he heard, Meitei interpreted it as some sort of “scheme.” “There was no scheme or anything of the sort. He merely told her to jump down from up there. Think of it: she is only a little girl of three or four, so of course she could not do such a wild thing.” “I see. That was much too lacking in ‘scheme.’ Still, he has no malice at heart; he is a good-natured man.” “If he had malice in his heart on top of everything else, I could never have gone on living with him.” The master's wife grew more and more vehement. “Come now, there is no need to be so dissatisfied. If you can get through each day in comfort like this, that is quite good enough. Kushami does not go out chasing amusements, and he does not fuss over clothes; he is a man perfectly suited to a plain, steady household life.” In a cheerful tone, Meitei delivered a sermon utterly unlike his usual character. “But you do not know. It is not like that at all...” said the master's wife. “Is he doing something behind your back? The ways of the world are hard to guard against, after all.” Meitei gave a breezy, drifting reply that missed the point entirely.

paragraphs.source_zh: 主人的妻子重新倒了茶，送到迷亭面前，说道：“让您受等啦，他大概快回来了吧。”“他上哪儿去啦？”“不知道呀，他这个人出门从来不说去哪儿，大概是到大夫那儿去了吧。”“是甘木大夫吗？甘木先生遇上他这种病人，算是倒霉啦。”看来主人的妻子无法回答，只好简单“唔”了一声。迷亭才不计较这些呢，又问道：“最近他怎么样？胃病稍微好些吗？”“好啊，坏啊，我一点也摸不清。就是甘木大夫再给他看上多少遍，像他那样一味吃果酱，我想他的胃病是好不了的。”主人的妻子把刚才对丈夫的不满，暗地向迷亭诉苦。“他那么爱吃果酱，简直成小孩子啦。”“不仅吃果酱，最近还狠命地吃萝卜泥呢，说什么这能治胃病。”“好家伙！”迷亭感叹地说。主人的妻子说：“他看了报纸，据说萝卜里有糖化酵母。”“原来是这样！这么说他是想用这种办法来抵消果酱啰，亏他想得出来。哈哈……”迷亭听了主人妻子的诉苦，反而流露出万分高兴的样子。“就在前几天，还给孩子吃呢。”主人的妻子说。“吃果酱？”迷亭问。“不，萝卜泥，您想不到吧？他说什么：‘小家伙，上这边来，爸爸给你好吃的。’难得他爱上一回孩子，可他竟然是这样地胡来。两三天前，他把二女儿抱上了衣柜……”“他又想出什么名堂来了？”迷亭不管听到什么事，都把它当作一种“名堂”来理解。“哪里是什么名堂不名堂，他只是让孩子从上边向下跳呀。您想想，只不过是个三四岁的小姑娘嘛，当然做不了那种疯丫头的事儿。”“原来是这样，这可太不成‘名堂’啦。不过，他这个人内心没有恶念，心地是善良的。”“假如内心里还有什么恶念，那我早就不和他一起生活啦。”主人的妻子气势越来越凶。“哈，你也用不着那样不满。像这样过着美满的小日子，蛮不错啦。苦沙弥这个人既不到外边去胡逛，也不讲究穿着，是个最适于老老实实过日子的人哩。”迷亭用一种快活的口吻，说了一番和他平日为人极不相称的大道理。“可是您不知道，完全不是这么回事儿……”主人的妻子说。“他瞒着你搞什么啦？真是世上人心难测啊。”迷亭飘飘然回答了一句不着边际的话。
